title: Tree of life – systematic biology and evolution
blurb: History of evolutionary thought: Lamarck (striving toward perfection, inheritance of acquired traits), Darwin (HMS Beagle, natural selection, 1858 with Wallace, On the Origin of Species 1859), Mendel (laws 1865–66, rediscovered 1900), the modern synthesis (1920s–40s; Dobzhansky's "nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution"), evo-devo and the extended synthesis.
h1: Tree of life – systematic biology and evolution
lede: History of evolutionary thought: Lamarck (striving toward perfection, inheritance of acquired traits), Darwin (HMS Beagle, natural selection, 1858 with Wallace, On the Origin of Species 1859), Mendel (laws 1865–66, rediscovered 1900), the modern synthesis (1920s–40s; Dobzhansky's "nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution"), evo-devo and the extended synthesis. Microevolution: natural selection (3 conditions, adaptation, steps), stabilising, disruptive and directional selection (peppered moth), sexual selection (giraffe necks, peacocks), mutation, gene flow, genetic drift (bottleneck, founder effect), domestication. Macroevolution: speciation (allopatric; adaptive radiation in Galápagos finches and cichlids; gradualism vs punctuated equilibrium), extinction, the history of life as a 24-hour clock, and the five mass extinctions.

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.a: A tendency toward perfection and the inheritance of acquired traits.

items.n: How would Lamarck explain the giraffe's neck?
items.a: Giraffes stretched their necks, and the longer neck was passed on to offspring.

items.n: When did Darwin sail on HMS Beagle?
items.a: 1831–1836 (Galápagos finches, South American fossils).

items.n: When did Darwin conceive natural selection?
Who published jointly with Darwin in 1858?
items.a: Alfred Russel Wallace.

items.n: When was On the Origin of Species published?
Where did Mendel work, and on what plant?
items.a: St Thomas' Abbey in Brno; peas (Fabaceae).

items.n: When were Mendel's laws proposed and rediscovered?
items.a: Proposed 1865–1866; rediscovered 1900.

items.n: What did the modern synthesis unite?
items.a: Natural selection and population genetics based on Mendelian inheritance (1920s–1940s).

items.n: Who said "Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution"?
items.a: Theodosius Dobzhansky (1973).
Evolutionary developmental biology: how evolution acts on development (e.g. Hox genes).

items.n: What does the extended evolutionary synthesis add?
items.a: Non-genetic inheritance: epigenetics, parental effects, ecological and cultural inheritance (memes).
Micro: small allele-frequency changes within a population. Macro: large-scale, long-term change incl. new species.
Natural selection, mutation, gene flow, genetic drift.
Variation in a trait, heritability of the trait, differential reproduction.
A heritable trait that enables organisms to survive and reproduce.
Intermediate forms favoured; human birth weight, clutch size.
Both extremes favoured, intermediates eliminated (rare); bill size in African finches.
Shift in one direction; peppered moth industrial melanism.
The increase of dark peppered moths (Biston betularia) in polluted Industrial-Revolution Britain, due to bird predation.

items.n: According to the lecture, why do giraffes have long necks?
items.a: Sexual selection: males fight with their necks, not reaching tall trees.
Female choice and male–male competition.

items.n: Can the environment create favourable heritable traits?
items.a: No; selection only acts on alleles already present (new ones arise by mutation).

items.n: Three responses of a population to environmental change?
items.a: Migrate, be already adapted, or die (local extinction).
Movement of alleles by emigration and immigration.

items.n: What is genetic drift, and where is it strongest?
items.a: Random change in allele frequencies by chance; strongest in small populations.
Drift after a sudden drop in population size, e.g. a catastrophe.
Loss of variation when a new population is founded by very few individuals.
No, domestication is artificial selection.
Divergence of one species into two or more descendant species.
Rapid diversification of one ancestral line; Galápagos finches, Lake Tanganyika cichlids.
Gradualism: continuous slow change. Punctuated: long stasis with sudden change.
3.6–3.8 billion years ago.

items.n: On a 24-hour clock of Earth's history, when do modern humans appear?
items.a: About 2 seconds before midnight.

items.n: Define a mass extinction. How many have there been?
items.a: Loss of > 75 % of organisms in a short time; five.
